title: Modernizing the World's Largest QSR Supply Chain
summary: I led the design of an enterprise-grade logistics platform for the world's largest QSR, leveraging AI to enhance predictive ordering and consolidating three legacy systems into one.
problem: Operators were juggling three legacy supply-chain tools daily. Forecasts were opaque, trust was zero, and stockouts were measured in millions of dollars per quarter.

items.title: Embed
items.body: Two weeks shadowing operators across four regions to map the real workflow.

items.title: Reframe
items.body: Shifted the goal from 'better forecasts' to 'forecasts operators trust' — a UX problem, not an ML problem.

items.title: Co-design
items.body: Built the recommendation surface with operators in the room, exposing the why behind every number.

items.title: Roll out
items.body: Region-by-region migration with a parallel-run safety net before each legacy tool was sunset.

challenge:
The world's largest QSR ran its supply chain on three overlapping legacy platforms — each owned by a different team, each with a different data model. Operators toggled between tools daily to plan orders, leading to stockouts, over-orders, and millions in waste.

Leadership wanted a single pane of glass: a modern, AI-assisted platform that could ingest historical demand, weather, and promo data and surface a confident order recommendation operators could trust.
approach:
I embedded with operators across four regions for two weeks of contextual interviews. The takeaway: nobody trusted the existing forecasts because the math was opaque. Trust — not accuracy — was the real constraint.

So we built a recommendation surface that always showed the why behind a number: trailing demand, anomalies, and editable assumptions. The model became a teammate, not an oracle.

flow.title: System consolidation
flow.sub: Three overlapping platforms, each owned by a different team with its own data model, replaced by one.
flow.note: All three were sunset within twelve months of launch.

dumbbell.title: Regional manager sentiment
dumbbell.sub: NPS among regional managers, historically a vocal critic group, before and after rollout.
dumbbell.note: NPS runs from −100 to +100; the axis is clipped to −50…+50 to keep the change readable.

outcome: Three legacy tools were sunset within twelve months of launch. Forecast accuracy improved 27% and operator onboarding time dropped nearly in half. Most importantly, NPS among regional managers — historically a vocal critic group — flipped from −12 to +44.
challenges: Three engineering teams with conflicting data models and incentives.
A vocal regional-manager group burned by previous tech rollouts.
Legal and compliance gates on AI-assisted decisions for high-volume orders.

quote.text: For the first time in a decade, I'm not double-checking the system in a spreadsheet.

lessons: Trust beats accuracy. A 90%-accurate model people use crushes a 95%-accurate model they don't.
Sunsetting legacy tools is a change-management project, not an engineering project.
Showing the math — even messy math — earns more buy-in than hiding it behind a confidence score.

title: Innovating the Consumer Debt Landscape, 0 to 1
summary: As the second product hire at a fintech startup, I led the strategy and launch of a B2B SaaS platform for consumer debt resolution, exceeding initial revenue targets by 80%.
problem: A $14B U.S. industry was running on faxes and spreadsheets. The startup had a wedge hypothesis, eight weeks of runway, and no shipped product.

stages.title: How I worked it
stages.sub: Four moves from nothing to a platform.

items.title: Narrow the wedge
items.body: One workflow (settlement offer routing) for one buyer (mid-market collection agencies).

items.title: Sales-as-discovery
items.body: Every demo was an interview; every objection became a backlog item.

items.title: Price on outcomes
items.body: Packaged on dollars resolved — not seats — to bypass the procurement gauntlet.

items.title: Platform expansion
items.body: Used the wedge as a beachhead for a broader creditor-side platform.

challenge:
U.S. consumer debt resolution is a $14B industry running on fax machines and spreadsheets. The startup's bet: replace the back office with a modern SaaS layer that could plug into both creditors and collection agencies.

I joined as the second product hire with no shipped product, no design system, and no defined ICP — just a wedge hypothesis and an eight-week runway extension.
approach:
We ran a deliberately narrow first release: one workflow (settlement offer routing) for one buyer (mid-market collection agencies). I built a sales-engineering loop where every demo became a discovery interview and every objection became a backlog item.

Pricing was packaged around outcomes — dollars resolved, not seats — which let us land enterprise pilots without a procurement gauntlet.

meter.title: Revenue against plan
meter.sub: Year one, indexed to the revenue plan.
meter.caption: of the year-one revenue plan
meter.note: Indexed to plan, set to 100. Derived from the reported 80% overperformance; absolute revenue figures are not published.

outcome: We blew past the year-one revenue plan by 80% and closed seven enterprise pilots in twelve months. The wedge product became the entry point for a broader platform play that's still expanding today.
challenges: Heavily regulated space with state-by-state compliance variance.
Two-sided market — neither side wanted to move first.
Existing vendors with deep, ugly integrations into customer back offices.

quote.text: Max ran our first ten enterprise deals like a designer — every objection ended up in the product within a week.

lessons: A wedge isn't a feature — it's the smallest contract you can close in 90 days.
Pricing is the fastest product lever a 0→1 team has.
If procurement is the bottleneck, you're selling at the wrong altitude.

title: Cross-Functional OKRs for a Hyper-Scale Startup
summary: As a Delivery Lead, I architected a cross-functional OKR framework to align priorities for a hyper-growth startup, boosting goal completion rates and reducing team friction.
problem: Post Series C, headcount doubled in nine months. OKRs existed on paper but planning had become a tug-of-war over engineering capacity.

items.title: Two-layer model
items.body: Company bets set top-down; squad commitments built bottom-up against those bets.

items.title: Dependency forum
items.body: A 30-minute weekly standup that surfaced cross-team blockers in week one.

items.title: Kill the deck
items.body: Replaced a 30-page planning deck with one shared doc and one shared scoreboard.

items.title: Coach the leaders
items.body: Worked 1:1 with each squad lead on writing measurable, falsifiable KRs.

challenge: After a Series C, the company doubled headcount in nine months. OKRs existed on paper, but every team wrote them in isolation — so quarterly planning devolved into a tug-of-war over engineering capacity.
approach:
I introduced a two-layer model: company bets (set top-down) and squad commitments (set bottom-up against those bets). A lightweight weekly forum exposed dependencies early instead of at the end of the quarter.

We killed the 30-page planning deck. In its place: a single shared doc, a shared scoreboard, and a 30-minute Friday standup.

dumbbell.title: Before and after, two quarters
dumbbell.sub: Completion rate rose while the planning cycle shortened.
dumbbell.note: Both rows share a 0–100 scale: completion is a percentage, planning cycle is days. They are plotted together because both moved in the intended direction over the same two quarters.

outcome: Goal completion nearly doubled and cross-team blockers fell 63% within two quarters. The framework outlived me — it's still how the company plans today.
challenges: Eleven squads with eleven planning rituals — none of them compatible.
Leadership wanted speed; ICs wanted predictability. Both were right.
A culture that confused activity with progress.

quote.text: Two quarters in, planning stopped being the thing we dreaded. That alone was worth it.

lessons: Goals don't fail at the goal-setting meeting. They fail at the dependency you didn't write down.
The shortest planning cycle that surfaces real conflict is the right one.
Operating frameworks are software — they need owners, releases, and bug fixes.

title: 4x-ing PayPal's Digital Value Chain
summary: How I led the product strategy and development of a new enterprise content management system for PayPal, increasing content velocity by 4x and boosting conversions by 40%.
problem: PayPal's marketing org spanned dozens of regions piped through a decade-old CMS. A single campaign change could take six weeks to ship globally.

items.title: Composable blocks
items.body: Decomposed pages into governed, reusable blocks owned by regional teams.

items.title: Paved road
items.body: An opinionated workflow for the 80% of campaigns that fit a standard pattern.

items.title: Off-road lane
items.body: A clearly fenced workflow for the 20% of campaigns that needed custom engineering.

items.title: Governance ≠ gatekeeping
items.body: Brand and compliance baked into the system, not enforced by review queues.

challenge: PayPal's marketing org spanned dozens of regions and product lines, all funneling through a single overworked CMS that hadn't been seriously rearchitected in nearly a decade. A campaign change in one market could take six weeks to ship globally.
approach:
We rebuilt the system around composable content blocks owned by regional teams, with a global governance layer that enforced brand and compliance without bottlenecking publishing.

I championed a 'paved road' for the 80% of campaigns that fit a standard pattern, and a clearly fenced 'off-road' workflow for the 20% that needed custom engineering.
